text:
Sam: Quick check — we need to pick an internal endpoint shape for routing policies, quotas, and console UX. Two options in play: (A) REST gateway that accepts JSON/proto-over-HTTP and centralizes routing/quotas in the gateway; (B) end-to-end gRPC+protobuf with sidecar/router enforcement. Which do we lean toward and why?
Priya: I'm +1 on gRPC for latency and typed contracts, but browser/console UX is clunkier. Need a good transcoding story.
Jonas: Gateway wins for observability/UI because it already aggregates per-route metrics. Easier to show token/latency breakdown in Console without instrumenting every service.
Maya: Quota enforcement at gateway makes billing and reserved capacity predictable. But single gateway enforcer = bigger blast radius on a config bug.
Sam: Agree. Also thinking of rollout patterns — gateway-based rollouts let us flip routing weights in one place. With sidecars we'd need a coordinated rollout everywhere.
Priya: Can we compromise? gRPC between services, gateway edge does HTTP->gRPC translation and does policy enforcement. That keeps internal perf and gives Console a single telemetry ingress.
Jonas: That is basically the adapter pattern. Downsides: gateway must understand proto versions and/or do transparent passthrough for unknown fields.
Maya: Proto evolution is a pain with translation. If we rely on gateway translation we need strong integration tests. Also we must expose trace IDs and quota tags through translation.
Sam: Quick data point: a small payload we measured — protobuf binary ~6.8KB, JSON ~13.5KB for same structure; median p99 token processing difference ~8-12ms on our infra. Numbers matter for cost.
Priya: On the console side, devs want per-route quotas and a simple 'simulate request' button. That requires either the gateway to expose route metadata or centralized metadata service.
Jonas: If gateway owns metadata, Console can query it for live SLO/quota state. If metadata is distributed (sidecars), console needs to aggregate. Both feasible but tradeoffs.
Maya: Security/compliance: private customers like pinned model versions + VPC. Gateway simplifies access control enforcement for those customers.
Priya: Another ops concern: schema evolution. With gRPC+proto-first we get compile-time guarantees. With JSON we're more tolerant but risk subtle contract drift.
Sam: For rollout UX — we should support canary weights + automatic fallback to a compatible model variant. Gateway-based routing makes that trivial to implement. Sidecar approach requires control plane rollout to update sidecars.
Priya: Proposal: adopt hybrid: gRPC+protobuf inside infra, gateway does strict translation and policy enforcement at edge, and a small metadata/compat service ensures gateway knows model version compatibility.
Jonas: I'd add: require gateway to forward X-Trace, X-Quota-Keys, and a route-id header. That keeps telemetry consistent and lets Console build per-request breakdowns.
Maya: Implementation notes: add integration test that replays protobuf golden fixtures through gateway translation and asserts byte-preserving passthrough for unknown fields. Fail fast on translation regressions.
Sam: UX ask: Console team — can you sketch a minimal wireframe that shows 'route-level quotas' + 'recent rollouts' if gateway exposes route metadata? @Priya will follow up. :thumbsup:
Priya: Yep. I'll spin up an initial mock tomorrow.
ops-bot: Canary started for gateway-policy v2 (canary id=gw-pol-2026-08, 5% traffic)
deploy-bot: deployment gw-pol-2026-08 succeeded in us-west-2 :rocket:
Sam: Cool — let's treat this hybrid model as the default in the RFC and call out the failure modes (gateway translation bugs, latency tail risks) with mitigation steps.
Maya: Agreed. I'll draft the test matrix for translation and quota enforcement.
Jonas: I'll prototype the minimal headers and a tiny telemetry endpoint for Console to poll.
Priya: Will attach the mock and a short matrix of pros/cons in the RFC PR.
Sam: Perfect. Thanks all.
